title: Defence spending and its short and longer-term macroeconomic effects (Economic Bulletin, Issue 6/2026)
key_claim: ECB staff note that purchases of large military equipment are recorded as defence spending only on delivery, so recording lags the spending; NATO figures are largely cash-based while national accounts record expenditure when economic ownership changes; the gap can be substantial in individual years during re-arming and tends to diminish in the long run; the macroeconomic impact hinges on the supply-side response.
frame_summary: ECB staff treat defence outlays as a macroeconomic shock whose size and timing depend on delivery lags and on how far supply can respond, not on budget announcements alone.

verbatim_list: when economic ownership changes, not when payments are made

title: EU economic governance framework indicators: national co-financing of EU programmes and defence expenditure (Statistics Explained)
key_claim: Eurostat says the Council has activated the national escape clause for 18 EU countries, with the allowed deviation for defence expenditure limited to a maximum of 1.5% of GDP during 2025-2028; COFOG defence data follow the national-accounts accrual time of recording, so equipment enters on delivery, while NATO payment-based data can show it earlier, at the time of a downpayment.
frame_summary: Eurostat presents the clause and the accrual convention as the measurement frame under which Member States' defence data and fiscal-rule compliance are read.

title: COM(2026) 495 final: Recommendation for a Council Recommendation on Greece's national escape clause for defence and energy security
key_claim: For Greece the clause applies until 2028; in the years after 2028 Greece may still exceed the maximum growth rates of net expenditure only to the extent the excess is related to deliveries of military equipment contracted before end-2028, within an overall cap of 1.5% of GDP; energy-security measures are added at 0.3% of GDP a year and 0.6% cumulatively.
frame_summary: The Commission frames the clause as temporary fiscal room through 2028 whose only post-2028 carry-over is tied to the contract date of military equipment, and widens its scope to energy security within the same cap.

verbatim_list: Until 2028, Greece is allowed to exceed the maximum growth rates of net expenditure
does not exceed 1.5 percent of GDP

notes: WebFetch 28/10/2026 of the copy of the Commission document held by the Austrian Parliament. A recommendation addressed to Greece only; the wording is read here as the instance of the rule, and the other 17 national texts were not tested.

title: Deutlicher Anstieg bei den Verteidigungsausgaben
key_claim: The draft 2027 federal budget raises defence expenditure to 139.6 billion euros; military procurement is to reach more than 60 billion euros in 2027, against 45 billion euros planned in the current year.
frame_summary: The Bundestag's own report on the 2027 draft budget presents procurement as the fastest-growing defence line.

title: Independent fiscal institution warns Lithuania faces a risk of non-compliance with fiscal rules (opinion on the Annual Progress Report 2026)
key_claim: Lithuania's independent fiscal institution says advance payments for defence are already increasing debt but will only be reflected in the deficit in the future, that the deficit could reach around 3% of GDP in 2028 and exceed it in 2029, and that the country will have to choose between funding defence and cutting other expenditure.
frame_summary: A national fiscal watchdog argues that defence procurement paid for now shows up in the deficit later, so compliance pressure peaks after the clause period ends.

title: European defense one year on: Money is not the problem, capacity (and delivery) are
key_claim: Allianz Trade economists say industrial investment and delivery have yet to catch up with spending, that backlogs stand at more than five times revenue while the capex ratio has stalled near 5%, that Europe's import ratio rose from 20% in 2021 to 45% in 2025, and that missile import prices are up 116% on the 2019-2021 average.
frame_summary: Allianz Trade argues the binding constraint on European rearmament is industrial capacity and delivery, not funding.
verbatim_quote: Backlogs stand at more than five times revenue while the capex ratio has stalled near 5%.

title: The Fiscal Timing of Europe’s Defence Purchases
key_claim: A specialist newsletter reports that Finland's October 2026 excessive-deficit notification carries a 'time adjustment of military expenditures' of 1.487 billion euros for 2025, down from 1.756 billion euros in the April notification, and argues that a government can authorise, contract, pay and borrow years before equipment is recorded as expenditure.
frame_summary: The newsletter argues that announced defence budgets and recorded deficits follow different schedules, which public accounts only partly let a reader reconstruct.
verbatim_quote: Finland reported a “time adjustment of military expenditures” of €1.487 billion for 2025.
verbatim_list: the April notification had put it at €1.756 billion
